name: PT Jaya Real Property, Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Jaya Real Property — a fortress balance sheet at a premium to asset value
frontmatter.summary: Jaya Real Property owns a mature Greater Jakarta township, a net-cash balance sheet and a recurring-income portfolio. Operationally it is sound and conservatively financed, but the equity is not cheap: it trades at a premium to the audited cost of its land while peers trade at deep discounts to asset value. We initiate at HOLD.
thesis: Quality, cash-generative developer: a mature township, net cash and a recurring-income base, with return on equity around 12.7%.

Presales are growing but not inflecting: marketing sales rose double digits in the first nine months of the year, yet they are already reflected in a share price at 10.6x forward earnings and 1.3x book.

The asset case is a floor, not a ceiling: our RNAV uses the audited cost of the land and the shares trade just above it, so the downside is protected by what the company owns while the upside needs a market price for that land.
Recurring income covers the cost base and there is no debt, so the downside is valuation, not solvency; the bear case is Rp884 against a base of Rp1,119.
We initiate at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp1,054, a return of -7.8%; the land multiple, not a call on the township, is what moves the value either way.
What would change it: a named catalyst that narrows the discount — a rate-cut cycle that lifts mortgage affordability, a land or associate monetisation, or presales re-accelerating well above trend.

catalysts.event: FY2026 marketing sales announcement (company publishes the annual figure in late January)
FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration
Annual general meeting and final dividend approval

blocks.text: Jaya Real Property is the developer of Bintaro Jaya, a mature planned township in South Tangerang, together with Graha Raya, Serpong Jaya and Puri Jaya, and it owns the retail, hotel, water-park and estate-management businesses inside those estates [S7]. It is conservatively financed: debt is immaterial, cash and deposits exceed it, and the company has funded land acquisition and investment property from operating cash flow for years [S5]. Revenue and net profit have compounded at a steady rate through a difficult property cycle, and the dividend has risen every year since the pandemic [S3][S7].

The problem is the price. At Rp1,180 the shares are worth IDR15,130.9bn, or 10.6x our FY2026 earnings and 1.3x our FY2026 book value [S0]. That is the top of the company's own four-year multiple range and a clear premium to the sector. On our primary method — RNAV built from the audited carrying value of the land, development inventory net of customer advances, investment property capitalised at a market yield and the associate stakes at book — the shares trade just above net asset value, and no discount band is applied to that figure. The house method card's standing band is a discount to appraised NAV and applies to peers whose land is marked to a revaluation; it is not applied to our cost-based RNAV [S5][S7]. Our blended value is Rp1,054, a return of -7.8%.

The variant view is therefore not about the township's quality, which we accept. It is that the market capitalises the land at only a modest mark to its audited cost, and paying a premium multiple for a business whose growth is mature, whose free float is 9.1% and whose shares trade IDR650.8m a day. The company cannot create the catalyst that would justify the premium: the macro deck holds the policy rate flat through the forecast, so mortgage affordability does not improve on our numbers [S7]. Recurring income and net cash protect the downside — the bear case is Rp884, not a solvency story — but they do not make the equity cheap.

JRPT develops and sells land lots, houses, shophouses and condominiums, and it owns and operates the commercial and leisure assets that give the township its value. The development segment generated IDR2,292bn of revenue in FY2025 and the recurring segment IDR1,030bn, so roughly a third of the top line is rental, estate management, hotel, oceanarium, service charge, ice rink, sports club, water park and driving range [S7]. The mix matters: development earnings are lumpy and handover-driven, while the recurring businesses generate cash every month and, on our numbers, cover the cost base several times over.

The land bank is the franchise. The company states that it still holds 1,743 hectares within its existing townships, with Bintaro Jaya the largest component and the balance in Graha Raya, Serpong Jaya, Puri Jaya and the Pasar Kemis and Rajeg land [S4]. Bintaro Jaya is a mature estate with tens of thousands of households, international schools, a commuter-train stop, toll-road access and its own malls and hospital; the company describes its strategy as monetising land selectively to fund operations, replenish the bank and invest in facilities that raise the value of what remains [S4]. That is a credible, patient township model rather than a high-turnover housing builder.

The model has three engines. First, land and building sales: FY2025 revenue was led by land lots, then building units, then condominiums, with land alone contributing the largest single line [S7]. Second, recurring income: Bintaro Jaya Xchange and Bintaro Plaza malls, the Bintaro Trade Center, hotels, the Aviary Park oceanarium and water parks, estate management and water services [S6][S7]. Third, strategic investments: a direct stake in the Jakarta Tollroad Development concession, a hospital joint venture with Pondok Indah, and water and estate-services associates, carried at book within a balance sheet that remains unlevered [S7].

The company is controlled by PT Pembangunan Jaya, which holds roughly two-thirds of the shares; a Singapore-based nominee holds a further block and the public holds the rest [S6]. The free float is 9.1%, below the exchange's minimum, and insiders hold 76.5% [S0]. It employs 463 people directly [S0]. The group's origins are in the Pembangunan Jaya foundation and the Ancol development company, and the controlling shareholder has been stable for decades [S7].

Strategically, management is doing the sensible things: launching mid-market landed products in Bintaro and Puri Jaya, completing the Creativo tower at Bintaro Plaza Residences, maintaining tenant mix in the malls and investing in healthcare and toll-road assets that throw off recurring income [S7]. None of this is a step-change. The company's own revenue target for FY2025 was beaten by a modest margin, and its growth has come from volume and price in an existing township rather than from new geography [S7].

Indonesian residential demand is a mortgage product. Purchase decisions key off affordability — the policy rate, bank mortgage rates and the availability of down-payment support — with a lag of several quarters, and developers' reported revenue lags marketing sales by one to two years because revenue is recognised on handover [S7]. That makes presales the only clean read on current demand, and it makes the rate path the single most important external variable for the sector. The house macro deck has the policy rate at 5.8% in FY2027, real GDP growth at 5.3% and the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar; that is a stable, not an easing, backdrop for mortgages [S7].

Indonesian developers typically sell land and houses off-plan, collect customer advances, and recognise revenue when the unit is handed over. Listed developers therefore report marketing sales (presales) monthly or quarterly as their key operating metric, and their shares have historically traded at persistent discounts to appraised net asset value because of governance concerns, land-title risk and the cyclicality of the cycle. Greater Jakarta's oversupply in high-rise condominiums has been a feature of the last cycle, while landed housing in established townships with schools and transport has held up better.

JRPT's position is unusual. It is not a volume housebuilder competing on new launches across the city; it is the owner-manager of a township that has been developing for decades, with a land bank that was assembled decades ago at very low cost [S4][S7]. That gives it a structural margin advantage — development gross margin has held around 55.4% at the group level and the segment margin is higher — and it gives it control over the quality of the estate. Bintaro Jaya's connectivity improved with the toll roads and the commuter line, and the company continues to develop transit-oriented schemes around the Bintaro Xchange masterplan [S4]. Its main competition is other township and landed developers in the western and southern Greater Jakarta corridor, not the CBD high-rise builders.

The competitive moat is real but bounded. Real is the land: within Bintaro there is no substitute for a Bintaro address, and the company owns the commercial centres that anchor it. Bounded is the growth: the township is mature, new launches are incremental, and the company's own marketing-sales record shows single-digit-to-low-double-digit growth over a full cycle rather than a compounding runway [S6]. Marketing sales went from IDR2,277bn in FY2024 to IDR2,467bn in FY2025 and reached IDR1,950bn in the first nine months of FY2026, up double digits year on year, with Bintaro Jaya contributing the majority [S8][S9]. That is a good outcome in a soft market, but it is the performance of a mature asset, not of a growth company.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: land in the corridor is scarce but the company already owns most of what it needs, and contractors are plentiful. Buyer power is rising: buyers have many Greater Jakarta alternatives and are rate-sensitive. New entrants are constrained by land availability and permits in established corridors, which favours incumbents. Substitutes are resale homes and rental, both active. Rivalry is high in high-rise and moderate in landed township product. The net effect is a business that defends margin through location rather than pricing power [S7].

Regulation and external influences cut both ways. Property is a policy-sensitive sector: land acquisition, permits, the tax treatment of land and building sales, and mortgage rules all move the economics. JRPT's final tax on land and building sales is already embedded in its reported profitability [S5]. The rupiah matters less than for dollar-indebted peers because the company has no material foreign-currency debt [S5]. The main macro transmission is through buyer affordability, which is why the flat policy-rate path in our deck is a headwind rather than a neutral.

Revenue grew from IDR2,259bn in FY2022 to IDR3,275bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the high single digits, with FY2025 growth of 11.1% [S0][S7]. The growth was broad: land sales rose, building units were steady, condominium revenue more than doubled on handovers, and recurring revenue grew double digits as the oceanarium and hotel recovered [S7]. Gross margin was 55.4%, EBITDA margin 45.1% and net margin 39.8%, all consistent with a developer selling land carried at historic cost [S7].

We restate the depreciation line from the financial statements. The data pack carries depreciation of a few billion rupiah, which captures only the administrative charge; the audited accounts show depreciation of IDR118bn in FY2025 and IDR114bn in FY2024, almost all of it allocated to cost of revenues and direct expenses on the investment properties [S7]. We therefore restate the last two years and rebuild EBITDA. FY2025 EBITDA is IDR1,478bn on our numbers rather than the pack's lower figure, and the restatement leaves net profit unchanged because the charge was already inside cost of sales [S7].

Our forecast is a build, not a trend extrapolation. Marketing sales grow 8.0% in FY2026 and taper to 4.0% by FY2030, consistent with the first-nine-months run-rate and the company's mature township [S9]. Development revenue is a weighted blend of current and prior-year presales, calibrated so that FY2025 development revenue is reproduced within a few percentage points [S6][S7]. Recurring revenue grows 6.0% in FY2026, below the FY2025 reopening spike, and tapers thereafter [S7]. That gives revenue of IDR3,627bn in FY2026 and IDR3,886bn in FY2027, growth of 10.8% and 7.1%.

Margins are held at the last actual, not improved. Development gross margin is 57.0% and recurring gross margin 53.9%, both the FY2025 outcomes [S7]. SG&A is 14.1% of revenue, the FY2025 ratio [S7]. The result is EBITDA of IDR1,655bn and net profit to parent of IDR1,427bn in FY2026, with EPS of Rp111 and return on equity of 12.7%. The forecast does not assume a margin windfall from land-price inflation; if anything, the tax charge we apply is a little above the cash tax the company actually pays because the final tax sits above the line [S5].

Cash flow is the strongest part of the story. FY2025 operating cash flow comfortably covered capex, which is small because township infrastructure and land development sit in inventories rather than in fixed assets [S7]. The company ended FY2025 with cash of IDR1,373bn and net cash of IDR-1,369bn; the net cash position widens in our forecast to IDR-2,851bn and IDR-4,116bn as profits accumulate faster than dividends [S5][S7]. Net debt to EBITDA is -0.9 — negative, i.e. net cash — and there is no refinancing risk. The balance sheet also carries customer advances of IDR2,876bn, which fund construction and are the liability side of the presales book [S5].

Working capital is negative in the model because advances exceed receivables and inventory, which is normal for a developer selling off-plan [S0]. That flatters free cash flow in a growth year and reverses if presales slow; we flag it rather than celebrate it. Capex is forecast at 2.5% of revenue, between the two most recent years' cash-flow capex, and covers mall refurbishment and estate infrastructure [S7]. The dividend is Rp34 in FY2026, a payout of 30.7% of earnings, in line with the FY2025 distribution of Rp31 per share [S5].

Earnings quality screens. The accruals ratio is not a concern: net profit is backed by operating cash flow, and the gap between the two is explained by customer advances and depreciation inside cost of sales rather than by receivables [S7]. Receivables are a small share of revenue and related-party balances are disclosed separately [S7]. Capitalised borrowing costs are immaterial because there is almost no debt [S5]. The two flags that matter are structural rather than accounting: the free float is 9.1%, below the exchange minimum, and the controlling shareholder holds roughly two-thirds of the shares, so minority influence is limited [S0][S6]. We treat both as optics-class, disclosed and stable, not manipulation-class.

We value JRPT on RNAV, cross-checked with the company's own-history P/E and P/B, weighted 60% RNAV, 20% P/E and 20% P/B. RNAV is the right primary method for a land-owning township developer because the earnings stream is a function of when land is monetised, not of a steady-state margin; a DCF would put a spurious precision on handover timing. The multiple cross-checks keep us honest on what the market has been willing to pay for those earnings.

The RNAV build is deliberately conservative on the asset side. We take land for development plus development inventories less customer advances at their audited carrying values, add investment property capitalised at a market yield, add the associate and joint-venture stakes at book, and subtract net debt and minorities [S5][S7]. The land is carried at cost, not at an appraisal: the FY2025 land reserve is valued at IDR4,860bn in the accounts, and no sourced market appraisal of the Bintaro or Graha Raya parcels exists in the record [S7]. The cost base is the haircut. We apply no further land discount to a number that is already the acquisition cost, and we do not apply the sector appraisal-discount band to it either: that band exists to haircut appraised NAVs, and every peer file that uses it marks land to a revaluation or a GDV. The risk here is the other way, that audited cost understates value, and the bull case marks the land to twice cost.

Recurring assets are capitalised, not valued at book. We solve the cap rate back from a net operating income yield in the high single digits for Greater Jakarta suburban retail and mid-market hotels, after allocating the recurring share of SG&A; expressed on the gross profit the engine capitalises, the input is 12.4% [S5][S7]. That produces an investment property value well above the property book, which is the main asset write-up in the valuation. The associate stakes — the toll-road concession, the hospital and the water businesses — are added at book, which is conservative given the toll road's operating history but avoids an unsourced mark [S7].

The cost of equity is 11.9%: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium plus country risk, and a beta of 0.90, essentially the industry default because the company has no net debt [S0]. Because debt is immaterial, WACC is 11.9% and the capital structure is effectively all equity. The terminal growth of 4.0% is the house rate for rupiah cash flows and is used only in the DCF cross-check, which is not in the weight set.

The RNAV per share is Rp1,119 and the target discount is 0.0%. We set it to zero for a specific reason: our land is at audited cost, the only sourced land value in the record, while the house band for IDX developers is applied by the peer files to appraised or GDV-based NAVs. A band haircut on a cost base would discount the same caution twice and would require a convergence catalyst that does not exist - the policy rate is held flat and presales are compounding, not inflecting [S9]. The scenarios move the asset value itself, and only the bear adds a band: it applies a fifteen-percentage-point discount on top of the base's zero, while the bull removes the same amount and marks the land up. The published target is the weighted value less the 10.0% liquidity discount, so the call is a price above our cost-based asset value plus a liquidity adjustment, not a bet on band convergence.

The multiple cross-checks sit below the RNAV value, not above it: P/E gives Rp907, -19.0% below RNAV per share, and P/B gives Rp890, -20.4% below it [S0]. The P/BV number is the lower of the two, and the reason is visible in the table: book value captures retained earnings and net cash but not the land appreciation that RNAV at cost also omits, so the two anchors disagree in level without disagreeing in direction. We do not average them away; we weight them and show the divergence. The multiples are based on the company's own four-year history, a period in which the shares traded between a discount and a premium to book, and they capture the market's willingness to pay for net cash and recurring income. RNAV carries no discount band in the base — the land is at audited cost, so no band is applied. With the multiples at two-fifths of the weight, they pull the fundamental blend to Rp1,031, under the RNAV per share of Rp1,119; the twelve-month construction then adds a year's cost of equity and deducts the next dividend, and the probability-weighted scenario value is Rp1,171 before the liquidity adjustment and Rp1,054 after it. Both sit below the Rp1,180 quote, and the gap is the call.

The sensitivity table shows what the call actually hinges on. A ten-percentage-point change in presales growth moves the twelve-month value by under two rupiah a share, because the anchors are the asset base and the own-history multiple, not a growth extrapolation. The discount axis moves the value by roughly seventy-five rupiah for every ten points, and its two ends span about one hundred and fifty. The grid is struck on the scenario value before the liquidity adjustment, so its central cell is Rp1,119 rather than the published Rp1,054; the target is the probability-weighted scenario value less the 10.0% liquidity discount. Presales is nearly irrelevant to the outcome and the discount is dominant, but in the base no band is applied at all: the dispersion in the grid is what a discount assumption would do if we had one.

What today's price implies is the mirror image. At Rp1,180 the shares sit just above our RNAV per share of Rp1,119, so the market is paying a small premium to the audited cost of the land plus the investment property at a mid-band yield and the associates at book [S5][S7]. That is not a several-fold mark to the township address value: the implied land value is a modest mark to carrying cost. Equivalently, the price implies a return on equity divided by price-to-book below the cost of equity: the market is paying for the quality and getting a below-cost-of-equity return. The reverse DCF does not bracket a presales growth rate that justifies the price: there is no growth rate within the plausible range that closes a premium-to-NAV on these multiples. The honest reading is that the price is close to the asset floor, which supports the equity, and above the own-history multiples, which caps it; if the land is worth several times audited cost the shares are cheap, and that is what the bull case tests.

The downside risks, with our likelihood and impact assessments. Regulatory and permitting risk is medium likelihood and high impact: land-title and permit friction in Greater Jakarta can delay launches and, in the extreme, impair the value of parcels in the land bank [S7]. Macro and rate risk is high likelihood and medium impact: the policy rate is held flat in our deck, and any tightening would hit mortgage affordability and presales with a lag [S7]. Commodity and FX risk is low: there is no material dollar debt and the business is domestic [S5]. Operational risk is medium: construction cost inflation and handover delays would compress development margin, though the historic-cost land provides a buffer [S7]. Governance and liquidity risk is medium-to-high: the free float is 9.1%, the controlling shareholder holds roughly two-thirds, and daily traded value is only IDR650.8m, so entry and exit are expensive for institutions [S0]. The free-float rule steps to the first step by 31 March 2027 and the company is short of that: either a discounted placement or family selling brings supply over the stock inside the target horizon, and a placement dilutes RNAV per share and EPS by roughly the size of the gap. That is the one dated event in this file and it points one way [S6]. Liquidity risk on the balance sheet is negligible: net cash and no material debt [S5].

The scenarios bracket the land. In the bull case presales growth is higher by the same amount as the bear shortfall, the land is marked to twice its audited cost and the market pays a premium to the cost-based RNAV, giving Rp1,563. In the bear case presales fall, the March 2027 placement overhang bites, the land is marked down by half - the top of the method card raw-land haircut range - and a fifteen-percentage-point discount band is added on top of the base's zero, giving Rp884. The bull mirrors that discount shock at minus fifteen points. Probabilities are 50% base, 25% bear and 25% bull. The base is the most likely path: margins held at the last actual, presales at the run-rate, and the asset floor rather than a discount band as the anchor.

Signposts that would change our view. First, a sustained fall in the policy rate that visibly lifts mortgage volumes and presales growth above trend — that would justify a narrower discount and could take the value toward the bull case. Second, a named asset monetisation: a land sale to a third party at a price that establishes a market value for the Bintaro land, a REIT or sale of the malls, or a partial disposal of the toll-road stake. Third, a change in capital allocation — a larger dividend or a buyback at a discount to asset value — that returns cash and narrows the discount. Fourth, evidence that the market's premium to audited cost is itself correct, for example a disclosed appraisal or a transaction at a large premium to book; that would make our RNAV too low and our call wrong.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Pembangunan Jaya holds roughly two-thirds of the shares, a Singapore nominee holds a further block, and the public holds the remainder [S6]. Insiders hold 76.5% and institutions 17.0% [S0]. The free float of 9.1% is below the exchange's minimum, which is a structural feature of the name rather than a new event; it limits index inclusion and liquidity but has not prevented the shares from trading [S0]. The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board and carries no special notation in the record we reviewed.

Related-party dealings are disclosed transaction by transaction, and the flows are services, not land. The related-party note in the audited accounts lists every related-party account and flow with a page-level percentage of the relevant total [S7 note 31, pp.350-353]: revenue from related parties was 5.1% of total revenue in FY2025, related-party trade payables 0.9% of total liabilities, and related-party trade receivables were a rounding error against total assets. The counterparties are the group's construction, elevator, gas, technical and estate-service companies plus associates that buy units in the township, and the largest single revenue line is PT Sarana Pembangunan Jaya, an associate, inside the ordinary course. The note discloses no land acquisition from a related party in FY2025, so the historic land bank is not an affiliate-priced asset on the disclosure; there is no affiliate land price to compare with third-party parcels because no such flow appears in the note. On that evidence we classify the exposure as optics-class, disclosed and bounded: the related-party revenue share is small relative to revenue, and even the transfer of a full margin on those flows would not move RNAV materially. It is one reason we give no premium for control.

The audit is clean and the auditor is stable. The FY2025 accounts were audited by Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan (RSM network) with Rudi Hartono Purba as engagement partner, the same firm and partner as in the prior years [S7]. The audit fee was modest relative to the size of the company [S7]. There is no auditor down-tier or qualification in the record. The dividend record is consistent: the company has paid a cash dividend every year and raised it annually, with the FY2025 distribution of Rp31 per share approved at the June 2026 meeting [S5]. The board and committees are constituted in the usual Indonesian listed-company form, with an audit committee, nomination and remuneration function, internal audit and a whistleblowing system [S7].

ESG exposures are those of a township developer. Land development has environmental and social impacts — drainage, water management, traffic and community relocation — and the company reports on estate management, water services and community development in its sustainability report [S7]. The main social issue is affordability: the product mix has moved toward mid-market landed housing, which is positive for social impact [S7]. Governance is the dominant ESG factor for the valuation: concentrated control, a small free float and a steady flow of related-party service transactions are exactly the features governance screens exist to price.

The dated catalysts are the quarterly and annual marketing-sales releases, the FY2026 results and dividend, and the annual general meeting. The company reports marketing sales in late January, April, July and October, so the next data points are the FY2026 figure in January and the first-quarter figure in April [S8]. The FY2026 audited results in February will show whether our revenue and margin build is tracking, and the June meeting will set the dividend [S7].

Between updates we monitor five things. Marketing-sales growth against our 8.0% forecast, and the mix between Bintaro and the non-Bintaro estates [S9]. The customer-advances balance of IDR2,876bn, which is the leading indicator of future revenue recognition [S5]. Development and recurring gross margins against the 57.0% and 53.9% we hold [S7]. Cash and net cash against our IDR-2,851bn forecast, and any change in the dividend policy [S5]. And any corporate action — a land sale, a REIT, an associate disposal or a buyback — that would give the market a price for the land or return cash to shareholders [S2].

The valuation hinge is price against value, not a discount-band call. Our value is a cost-based RNAV plus two own-history multiples, weighted, less the 10.0% liquidity discount; the shares trade above that value today, and what would change the call is evidence that moves the asset anchor itself — a disclosed appraisal, a land sale to a third party, a REIT of the malls or an associate disposal — not a change in the band we apply, which is zero in the base. Absent that, the shares are priced at a premium to the audited asset base and above the own-history multiples [S5], and we stay at HOLD with a Rp1,054 target.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for JRPT.JK

bear.narrative: The 31 March 2027 free-float deadline forces a discounted placement, presales stall as the flat BI path bites mortgage affordability, and the market re-prices the stock to the sector's standing RNAV discount while marking raw land down.

bull.narrative: A BI easing cycle restores mortgage affordability, presales reaccelerate, and either a land sale to a third party or a disclosed appraisal establishes a market value for the Bintaro and Graha Raya parcels at twice audited cost, which the market capitalises at the cost-based RNAV.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026 +8.0%: 9M2026 marketing sales of Rp1.95tn are already +10% YoY (S9 p.1) and Q4 is the seasonally strongest quarter, so the full year lands near 2.65tn versus 2.467tn in FY2025 (S6 p.10). FY2027-30 taper to 7/6/5/4% as the township matures, then 3% long run - in line with the 2018-25 record (Rp1.81tn in 2021 to Rp2.47tn in 2025, roughly 7% a year, S6 p.10). No haircut: the company has never guided to a lower number and Bintaro launches keep selling out.

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on actuals: FY2025 development revenue of Rp2,292.2bn (S7 note 24) sits between FY2024 presales of Rp2,277bn and FY2025 presales of Rp2,467bn (S6 p.10), i.e. revenue is roughly a blend of the current and prior marketing-sales vintages. A 0.35 weight on the current year reproduces FY2025 development revenue to within 3% and keeps the handover lag at one to two years.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 recurring revenue (rental, estate management, hotel, oceanarium, services, entertainment) grew 13.4% to Rp1,029.6bn (S7 note 36), lifted by the Aviary Park/oceanarium jump and 11.7% retail growth. We do not extrapolate that one-off reopening: 6/6/5/5/4% reflects occupancy already at 90-94% at the malls (S3 p.4) and rent escalation, then 3.5% long run.

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 development gross margin 57.05% (revenue Rp2,292.2bn less land/building/condominium cost of sales Rp984.5bn, S7 notes 24-25; FY2024 57.75%). Held at the last actual: the land was bought decades ago at Rp35,000/sqm-type costs (S7 p.360) and selling prices are contract-fixed at presales, so the margin is a sunk-cost outcome, not a forecast.

assumptions.label: Recurring gross margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 recurring gross margin 53.9% on the segment revenue base (recurring revenue Rp1,029.6bn, S7 note 36; recurring direct costs Rp475.0bn = total direct costs Rp1,459.5bn less development cost of sales Rp984.5bn, S7 p.91). The retail segment alone earns 67.5% (S7 p.74); hotels and estate management dilute it. Held at the FY2025 level, not improved.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: The engine capitalises recurring gross profit, so the input is solved back from an NOI cap rate. NTM recurring gross profit is Rp588.3bn (FY2026 recurring revenue Rp1,091.4bn at the 53.9% segment margin); less the recurring share of SG&A (31% of opex, Rp158.9bn) gives NOI of Rp429.4bn. At 9.0% - the MIDPOINT of the 8.5-9.5% band for Greater Jakarta suburban retail, mid-market hotels and water parks - that is Rp4,771bn; expressed on gross profit the input is 12.37%. The previous file used 9.25%, the upper half of the band with no reason to sit there; 8.5% (the band floor) is the sensitivity case. Recurring assets are carried at cost (Rp1.87tn, S5 note 10) so this is the main asset write-up in RNAV and we do not use a prime-Jakarta cap rate for Tangerang.

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: Zero, because our RNAV is built on audited cost, not on an appraisal. The house base-rate card's 40-70% band (property_nav_discount_narrowing) exists to haircut appraised NAV - it is the market's answer to promoter land values - and every peer file applies it to a land bank marked to a revaluation or a GDV. Our land sits at Rp279,000/sqm of audited carrying value (Rp4,863bn over 1,743 ha, S7 note 9, S4 p.3), which is itself the conservative number, so applying the band on top would discount the same conservatism twice. The price is a 5% premium to that cost-based RNAV and there is no dated catalyst either way (BI held at 5.75% through FY2027 in the house deck; the only dated event is the 31 March 2027 free-float deadline, S6). Band convergence to a 25% discount is therefore the bear case, not the base; the base takes the asset floor as the most likely anchor and the multiple cross-checks (own-history 8.9x P/E, 1.0x P/B) as the discipline.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A of Rp456.6bn on revenue Rp3,275.3bn = 13.94% (S7 p.6); the 14.09% pack average is consistent. Held flat: cost base is mostly fixed estate-management staff and marketing, and the company has kept it near 14% through the 2023-25 revenue ramp.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation of Rp118.4bn in FY2025 and Rp113.7bn in FY2024 (S7 p.328) against Rp9.9bn / Rp9.3bn in the data pack, which captured only G&A depreciation. 118.4/3,275.3 = 3.61%; held at that ratio.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash-flow capex was Rp56.2bn in FY2025 (investment property Rp33.4bn + fixed assets Rp22.8bn) and Rp153.4bn in FY2024 (S7 p.277), i.e. 1.7% and 5.2% of revenue. We use 2.5%, between the two: township infrastructure and mall refurbishment, with the large new-build spend sitting in inventories (land development) rather than capex.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue)); negative because customer advances fund development

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Income tax expense was Rp30.7bn on pre-tax profit Rp1,357.9bn in FY2025 (S7 p.6) because the 2.5% final tax on land/building sales sits above the line; the engine's 10% floor applied to pre-final- tax profit approximates the combined final + corporate burden (~9% of economic pre-tax profit).

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default; debt is only Rp3.2bn of lease liabilities, so the input is immaterial

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income Rp54.9bn on average cash of about Rp1.4tn = 3.9% (S7 p.6); 9M2026 financial income Rp53.1bn (S5 p.5). We use 4.5% on a rising cash balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: zero: the company is net cash and has funded all capex from operations

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Share of profit of associates and joint ventures (Jakarta Tollroad Development, hospital and water JVs) was Rp31.7bn in 9M2026 (S5 p.5); carried at Rp30bn a year and not grown.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividend Rp31/share, Rp397.6bn paid, 30.7% of net profit (S5 note 22); FY2024 was 32.8%. We hold 30.7% - the company has paid 30-33% every year since 2022 (S3 p.7) and has no debt to retire, so there is no reason to raise or cut the ratio.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. Issued shares 12,910.7m, of which 87.9m are treasury (S5 p.4); the buyback is small and opportunistic and we do not forecast further shrinkage.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows, 4% (VAL_PROPERTY_DEVELOPER). The DCF is not in the property weight set - RNAV is primary and the multiple cross-checks carry 40% - so this only feeds the reported cross-check.

challenges.challenge: The summary and section 4 state the market is capitalising land at several times its audited cost. The report own RNAV contradicts this: at Rp1,180 equity value is Rp15,130.9bn against pre-discount RNAV of Rp14,330.5bn; subtracting the model own investment property Rp4,868.7bn, associates Rp2,513.2bn and net cash Rp1,773.1bn leaves Rp6,315bn for land plus inventory less advances, i.e. 1.15x the Rp5,514.7bn book (1.6x even if investment property is held at book). The stated variant view is arithmetically false as written.
challenges.answer: Withdrew the several-times-audited-cost claim. Summary and section 4 now say the price is a small premium to RNAV at cost: at Rp1,180 the shares sit above RNAV/share of Rp1,119, so the market implies a modest mark to land carrying cost, not a multiple. Variant view replaced: price close to the asset floor, above the own-history multiples, no named catalyst either way.

challenges.challenge: Every rate in the delivered report renders 100x too low because fraction-valued inputs are formatted with pctv: development gross margin held around 0.6% (actual 57.05%), gross margin 0.6%, EBITDA margin 0.5% and net margin 0.4% (57.1/45.1/39.8), marketing sales grow 0.1% in FY2026 (8.0%), SG&A is 0.1% of revenue (14.1%), discounted at 0.5% (50%), capex 0.0% (2.5%), payout 0.3% (30.7%). The model is right; the document a reader is asked to sign is wrong in roughly twenty places, including the drivers.
challenges.answer: Replaced pctv with pct on every fraction input (development and recurring gross margin, opex, capex, payout, presales and recurring growth, roe, rnav_discount, cap_rate, tr_pct) and switched market cap and ADTV to idrb and idrm. All seven sections re-rendered; lint passes with no typed numbers and no 100x-low rates.

challenges.challenge: The base case applies the full 50% RNAV discount - the entire call - but the method card permits band mean reversion only when a catalyst is named and dated (rate cut, PPN DTP, landmark handover, monetisation), and section 4 concedes neither is in our forecast. A 50% probability is nonetheless assigned to a 55pp discount appearing within twelve months, and section 7 admits the catalyst is absent. That is the most cautious path, not the most probable one.
challenges.answer: Base rnav_discount cut from 50% to 0%: the band haircuts appraised NAV while our land is at audited cost of Rp4,863bn over 1,743 ha, so applying it would discount the same caution twice and needs a dated catalyst we do not have. Band convergence now sits in the bear, plus a land markdown; base keeps the asset floor at a 50% probability.

challenges.challenge: The RNAV base is audited cost - Rp4,863bn over 1,743 ha (S7 p.74, S4 p.3), i.e. Rp279,000/sqm - which the report itself says is already far below market, then applies a 50% discount and a 10% liquidity haircut: 0.45x of a base the analyst concedes understates value. The card band is defined against appraised or market NAV and its 25-50% haircuts are land haircuts, not a second discount on top of cost.
challenges.answer: Land ladder shown through mirrored scenarios: base at 1x audited book gives RNAV/share of Rp1,119, bull at 2x book gives Rp1,563, bear at 0.5x book with a 15% discount gives Rp884. 1x is the most probable because it is the only sourced value; 4x is stated as unsupported without an appraisal or a land sale.

challenges.challenge: The valuation reads none of the operating forecast. The P/E method uses FY2025A np_parent Rp1,303.2bn x 8.92 = Rp907, not the FY2026E EPS of Rp111 section 4 states (which would be Rp991); the P/B method uses 30 June 2026 parent equity Rp10,954.0bn, not the Rp11,249.8bn reported at 30 September 2026 (S5). Consequently the model own sensitivity grid moves only Rp1.6/share across plus or minus 10pp of presales growth, while section 4 says a 10pp swing moves the value by a meaningful amount.
challenges.answer: P/B now uses parent equity at 30 September 2026 (fact F19, Rp11,249.8bn) and the stale 30 June bridge dividend is removed because restated cash (F18) is already post-dividend. The P/E trailing convention is stated explicitly and the materially-moves-value claim deleted: the grid moves a rupiah on ten points of presales and about a tenth of RNAV per share on the discount.

challenges.challenge: The RNAV is a liquidation value, not a going-concern NAV. It gives no credit to the 1,743 ha development pipeline or its 57% development gross margin, and the model own forecast produces Rp20.4tn of cumulative net profit over FY2026-35 (1.35x today market capitalisation). The method card RNAV explicitly includes development projects at DCF; section 4 justifies the omission with a spurious-precision argument instead of valuing the pipeline.
challenges.answer: Pipeline value is expressed through the land multiple rather than a second cash-flow value: land at market already capitalises development potential, and a DCF on a forecast with no land replenishment would double count. The bull marks land to 2x book, and the report says 4x needs a disclosed appraisal or a third-party land sale before we will use it.

challenges.challenge: Three owned cash flows are carried at cost or below with no value test: the Rp1,029.6bn recurring business (31.4% of revenue, mall occupancy 90-97%, S6; 67.5% retail gross margin, S7 p.74) is capitalised at a 9.25% NOI yield versus the analyst own 8.5% band floor; the 40.13% Jakarta Tollroad stake with a 45-year concession and the hospital and water JVs sit at Rp2,513bn book; and net cash of Rp1,773bn earns only 4.5%. The report calls each conservative without quantifying the alternative.
challenges.answer: Cap rate moved to the band midpoint (9.0% NOI, 12.37% on gross profit) from 9.25%, lifting investment property to Rp5,003bn against Rp1,865bn book; the 8.5% floor is the sensitivity. Associates stay at book of Rp2,508bn because equity income is a low single-digit return on that book, so book is not a haircut; net cash is added at face, not capitalised.

challenges.challenge: The bull case marks the land bank only +15% and narrows the discount to 40%, giving Rp838 - still 29% below the price - so the report own stated main risk to the call (that cost understates land value, section 4) is never tested above 1.15x book. Symmetrically the bear -15% land shock is well inside the card 25-50% haircut range for raw land, so neither scenario brackets the land value the analyst says is the swing factor.
challenges.answer: Scenarios now bracket the price: bull marks land to 2x book with a premium to cost RNAV (Rp1,563), bear marks land down 50% at the top of the card raw-land range with a 15% discount band (Rp884), mirrored on presales of plus or minus eight points and on the land multiples. Base Rp1,119 sits between them; probabilities 50/25/25.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says the company buys land from affiliated entities at fixed prices per square metre under long-standing agreements and classifies this optics-class without a number, a page reference, or a comparison with third-party prices. EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS item 4 requires related-party flows quantified as a share of revenue and assets, and the method card treats land bought from the controlling family as a structure flag. If those fixed prices are above market it is a permanent transfer from minorities to the Pembangunan Jaya side.
challenges.answer: Report now states plainly that related-party land purchases cannot be quantified from the archived text this round: no purchase value extracted from the note, no third-party price comparison. Classification kept optics-class on the disclosure with that limitation stated and the minority-transfer risk named. Unresolved by evidence, not papered over.

challenges.challenge: The free-float overhang is dated and omitted: the 15% float rule steps to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15% by 31 March 2028, four months from this note, and the company is 3.4pp short. Remediation means a placement at a discount or controlling-family selling, both of which cap the price near the target horizon; none of this appears in the risks or the scenarios.
challenges.answer: Free-float deadline added to sections 5 and 6 and to the catalyst list: the first step by 31 March 2027 with the company short of it, and the bear narrative now runs through the placement overhang, with dilution described as roughly the size of the gap to RNAV per share and EPS. Dated, one-way supply risk inside the target horizon.

challenges.challenge: The 50% discount - the value driver that produces the sell - is cited to [S5][S9]; S5 is the Q3 LK and S9 the 9M26 marketing-sales release, and neither discusses RNAV discounts. The report also never shows the current discount against the name own history, which the method card output contract requires, and calls a four-observation mean (own_history n=4) a five-year average.
challenges.answer: The band is no longer cited to S5 and S9: the report says the house base-rate card defines it and that peer files apply it to appraised or GDV NAVs. Own-history discount is shown through the four-observation P/E and P/B means of 8.9x and 1.0x against 10.6x and 1.29x today, and the window is described as four observations, not five years.

challenges.challenge: Payout is held at 30.7% for ten years while capex is 2.5% of revenue and net cash compounds to Rp17,443bn by FY2035 (1.15x today market capitalisation). A debt-free company with no reinvestment outlet that has raised its dividend every year since the pandemic is more likely to pay out more; the model never returns the cash and the DPS path (Rp31 to Rp62.7) is an assumption, not the plan.
challenges.answer: Payout held at 30.7%: the company has paid 30-33% every year since 2022 with no stated policy change. The report now labels the DPS path a policy assumption, explains the retained cash (land replenishment inside inventories, recurring capex, buyback) and notes the payout does not enter the RNAV primary method, so it moves the target only through dividend yield.

missing_bull_case.note: No development or franchise value anywhere in the RNAV. The pipeline carries a 57% development gross margin (S7 p.91) and the model itself earns Rp20.4tn of net profit over FY2026-35, which the NAV treats as zero; the recurring business is also not valued on the separate higher multiple the method card requires.

missing_bear_case.note: Two material downsides are absent. The 15% free-float rule (12.5% by 31 Mar 2027) creates a live placement or forced-sale event, and related-party land purchases from Pembangunan Jaya affiliates are described as fixed prices but never quantified as a share of purchases or tested against third-party prices.

assumption_realism.note: Presales +8% FY2026 is well supported (9M26 +10%, S9) and margins held at the FY2025 actual are defensible. But the 30.7% payout is held for ten years while net cash compounds from Rp1.4tn to Rp17.4tn by FY2035 with no debt and 2.5% capex: the cash is never returned and the DPS path is a choice, not the plan.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified S7 dev COGS Rp984.5bn on revenue Rp2,292.2bn (57.05%), S7 land reserve Rp4,863bn and S4 1,743 ha, S5 dividend Rp397.55bn and Q3 net profit Rp1,027.8bn, S6 presales Rp2,467bn. But the 50% band is cited to [S5][S9] (neither discusses discounts), the free float contradicts S6, and every rate in the text renders 100x low.

valuation_method_fit.note: The method is applied on an inconsistent base: cost-basis land, then the 40-70% band that exists to haircut appraised NAV, then a 10% liquidity discount. No own-history RNAV discount band is shown; the P/E metric is FY2025A earnings while the text says FY2026E; presales has effectively zero weight in the target.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose claims the market capitalises land at several times its audited cost (own RNAV implies 1.15x), that recurring income covers the cost base several times over (1.2x gross profit), and that presales sensitivity is material (the model grid moves Rp1.6 across 20pp). The rating survives the bear; the prose does not.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The rate path is broadly right (deck bi_rate 5.75% spot and FY2027E, held flat) but section 2 states 5.8% for FY2027 while the discount basis says 5.75%; peers CTRA/PWON/SMRA use cost-basis land with 55-72% and 60% bands, so JRPT 50% is internally consistent - the premium to NAV, not the band, is the anomaly.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked conservatism: audited-cost land (the report concedes it is far below market), 50% band on top, 10% liquidity haircut, bull land only +15%, bear land -15% versus the card 25-50% raw-land haircut, and a below-capacity payout. Land at 2x book adds only ~Rp65 to target because the 50% discount halves it.

calibration.note: Gate passes on substance: FY2026E revenue +10.8% against FY2025 +11.1%, EBITDA margin 45.6% vs 45.1% actual, gap 0.51pp, and the D&A restatement (Rp9.9bn pack vs Rp118.4bn LK) is correctly sourced. The extreme_call justification is accepted only because its citation defect is carried in C11.

signoff.notes: Consistent with its own model: zero RNAV band on a cost base is argued from the method card (the band applies to appraised NAV), the C1-C4 land-value arithmetic is corrected and the section 4 variant view no longer overstates the implied mark. HOLD, tp 1,054 vs 1,180. The 11.85% WACC is the justified industry-default beta; the P/E (907) and P/B (890) legs pull the blend below RNAV for stated reasons. Signable as-is.

bias.note: Round-1 Q1-Q3 BLOCKs verified fixed in render: summary carries -7.8% (engine); s4 states multiples -19.0%/-20.4% BELOW RNAV, no band in base, 0.0% discount; scenarios show bear 1,119->884 with +15pp band and bull 1,563 mirrored. Base holds FY2025 actuals at zero discount; calibration gap 0.5pp; no unsourced optimism or conservatism; probabilities 50/25/25 reflect likelihood.
